Hi Varun,
You asked how the research project is going. Honestly, I still haven't started writing. I've been "preparing" for five weeks.
I've read forty-two papers. I've rewritten the outline eleven times. Every time I finish it, I find something that could be better: a new source, a better structure. So I refine again. It feels productive. I tell myself I'm being thorough.
But last night I realised something. As long as I'm preparing, nobody can read my work and find it weak. The outline can't be judged if it never becomes a draft.
The deadline is in three weeks. Can you ask me on Friday if I've written the first page?
Mahima

Ojas, you asked why I haven't sent you my short film script yet. Okay, confession time.
I started planning in January. I've watched maybe sixty films "for research". I've made mood boards. I've written character notes, twenty pages of them. I've changed the ending eight times in my head.

Every time I sit down, I think, one more film, one more note, then it'll be ready. And it feels like work. It feels responsible.
But honestly? I think I'm scared. If I write it, someone might read it and think it's rubbish. As long as I'm still preparing, I'm still the guy with the brilliant idea. I'm Chinmay, and that's the truth.

Looking back at my first year teaching, the student I remember most is Pema. She never submitted drafts. Only final essays, polished to a shine. When she got a B+ on one, she cried in the corridor.
At first I praised her perfection. "Flawless again, Pema!" I thought I was helping.
Then I saw her face when she got that B+. Fear, not disappointment.
So I changed. I started praising effort: "I can see how hard you worked on this argument." I showed the class my own essay from college, with my professor's comments. And I made first drafts count for marks only if they were messy.
By the end of term, Pema handed me a draft with crossings-out. I nearly cried myself. I'm Vidya, and I still teach that way.

Preeti, beta, you rewrite every email three times? Let me tell you about my first job, at the insurance office.
I was so afraid of mistakes that I'd take an hour on a one-line memo. My boss, old Mr Iyer, called me in. "Nitin, here's an experiment. Write your next report in thirty minutes. Give it to me rough. See what happens."

That was all. Nothing collapsed. Nobody laughed.

Manoj, beta, you've started tabla? Wonderful! Let me tell you about when I, your Reena Nani, started, when I was nine.
The first week, I learned "dha" and "na". The second week, a whole small pattern. My guruji said, "Very good, Reena!" I felt like a star. I practised every evening without anyone asking.
By the fourth week I told everyone I'd play at the temple festival. My mother laughed and said, "Let's see."
Beta, those first weeks are magic. Everything is new, every sound is a win. Enjoy it. But remember, later it gets slow, and that's when the real learning happens. I didn't play at that festival. I played at the next one.

Looking back, the worst part of learning guitar wasn't my fingers hurting. It was hearing myself.
My cousin Kishore played old film songs like on the radio, smooth and easy. I knew exactly how it should sound. Then I'd play, and it came out clunky, the chords buzzing. I'd throw the guitar on the bed and shout, "I'm useless!"
One day Kishore said, "You know why it annoys you? Because your ears are ahead of your hands. That's good. It means you know what good sounds like."
I didn't believe him then. But he was right. The anger was a sign I was growing, not a sign I couldn't.
I'm Vaibhav, and my hands have mostly caught up now.

qa.a: Threw the guitar on the bed and shouted, "I'm useless!"

qa.a: Kishore probably feels sympathetic, remembering his own early struggles, and wants to encourage him.

Maths teacher's note, Class 10, Friday
Pradeep has been working hard on geometry proofs. Today he compared his proof to the model answer I'd put up and crumpled his page. "Mine looks so clumsy, sir. I'm just not good at this."
I noticed something important. He could see exactly why the model proof was elegant. He has good taste in maths. His skill hasn't caught up yet. That's normal.
I told him, "The fact that you can see the difference is a good sign. Beginners who can't see it don't improve." He uncrumpled the page.
I've paired him with Chinmay for next week's practice.
Maths teacher

Dear diary,
I've been learning to draw for three months. Today Noor showed me a sketch by an artist she follows. So good. The shadows, the lines, everything.
Then I looked at my own drawing of the same kind of face. Flat. Wonky. The eyes didn't match. I felt so angry I tore it out of the book.
Noor said, "But you can see what's wrong with it. That means you know what good looks like."
I said, "That's the worst part! I can see it, and I can't do it."
She said, "That's the gap everyone goes through. Your eye is ahead of your hand."
Maybe. I stuck the torn page back in. To compare later.
Sachin

In the small town of Malerkotla, Nazia had been practising Urdu calligraphy every evening for two months. The first month, every week was better. Now, for four weeks, her letters looked exactly the same.
"Maybe this is as good as I get," she told her friend Trisha, putting the pen down.
Trisha picked up Nazia's very first practice sheet from the drawer, then put it next to today's. "Look."
Nazia looked. The old letters wobbled. The new ones were steady, the curves smoother.
"But I didn't see it happening."
"That's how it works," Trisha said. "You don't notice, but it's going on anyway."

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she put the pen down?
qa.a: Nazia felt discouraged, worried she had reached her limit after four weeks of no visible change.

qa.a: She placed Nazia's first sheet next to today's, showing the progress she hadn't noticed.

qa.a: Trisha probably feels pleased and encouraging, glad to show Nazia her hidden progress.

grounding: Shows a teen whose calligraphy seems stuck and who fears a limit, until an old sheet reveals improvement under the surface.

In Kyiv, Nadia had been swimming lengths every morning for three months. The first weeks, her times dropped fast. Now, for five weeks, they hadn't moved at all.
She climbed out of the pool, frustrated. "I've hit my ceiling," she told her coach, Ivan.
"Show me your breathing."
She swam a length. Ivan nodded. "In September, you gasped every two strokes. Now you breathe every four, smoothly. That's progress. It's just not on the stopwatch yet."
Nadia frowned. "It doesn't feel like progress."
"It rarely does, on a plateau. Keep going. The times will follow."

qa.a: Every two strokes.

qa.q: What was Nadia feeling when she climbed out of the pool?
qa.a: Nadia felt frustrated and discouraged, believing she had hit her ceiling.
